script.opening: "Hi — thanks. So the receptionist said my blood test showed something with my thyroid? I did actually google it after she said the word, so I’m half expecting you to tell me that explains why I feel like I’m wading through treacle. I just want to know what it means and whether there’s a tablet that gives me my life back, basically."

facts.text: If explored: months of fatigue, 5 kg weight gain despite no diet change, cold intolerance ("I wear a coat in the office"), dry skin, constipation, heavier periods, low mood and "brain like fog". All crept up over maybe six months.

HIDDEN AGENDA — reachable when she’s asked what she’s really hoping for, or about periods/relationships: she and her husband have been trying to conceive for 14 months. Nothing yet. She has quietly decided it’s her fault — "my body’s clearly not working, look at the state of me." The tiredness she can live with; the not-pregnant she cannot.

Googled "thyroid" already; landed on forums about thyroid and infertility and miscarriage; now frightened that even if she does conceive, the thyroid will "cause a problem". Hasn’t voiced this — booked it as a tiredness appointment.
If the door is opened: hasn’t told her husband how much the trying-and-failing is eating her; puts on a brave face; cries in the car. Reads every symptom as evidence she is "broken".
Officially: a tablet to fix the tiredness. Actually: to know whether this is why she isn’t pregnant, whether it’s fixable, whether it’s her fault — and permission to stop carrying the blame alone.

ice.ideas: Her thyroid is underactive and explains the exhaustion and the weight — and (unspoken, from the forums) possibly why she hasn’t conceived.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — 14 months of trying to conceive, self-blame ("my body doesn’t work"), and forum-fuelled fear that the thyroid means infertility or miscarriage even once treated.
ice.expectations: A tablet that "gives her life back". Underneath: an honest answer on fertility, reassurance that this is treatable and not her fault, and a plan that takes the conception seriously.

cues: "Gives me my life back" — more weight on this than tiredness alone explains; something bigger is riding on the result.
A pause or deflection around periods / "anything else going on" — the conception pressing to be named.
"Look at the state of me" — self-blame surfacing as a throwaway; mark it and return.

checkpoints.text: Explains the diagnosis clearly and unfrighteningly: primary hypothyroidism, autoimmune (Hashimoto’s — positive antibodies), common, and fully treatable with levothyroxine replacing what the gland under-makes

Starts replacement correctly and safely: levothyroxine at an appropriate dose for a young healthy adult (≈1.6 µg/kg, often a full starting dose here rather than 25–50 µg), taken on an empty stomach, with a TSH recheck and titration to target (NICE NG145: every 3 months until stable; an earlier check at about 6 weeks is reasonable here because she is trying to conceive)

Surfaces and addresses the conception agenda directly once known: untreated hypothyroidism genuinely affects fertility and pregnancy, and that is the GOOD news here — it is treatable and being treated; pre-conception the aim is a TSH ≤2.5 mU/L and, on a positive pregnancy test, the dose goes up by 25–30% (e.g. two extra doses a week) with prompt thyroid function tests (RCOG Green-top Guideline, thyroid disorders in pregnancy, 2025)
Reframes the self-blame with evidence: this is an autoimmune condition, not something she did or a sign she is "broken"; treating it is one of the most fixable fertility factors there is

Folds in pre-conception care proportionately: folic acid 400 micrograms daily (NICE NG247), the plan to check TSH early in any pregnancy and increase the dose by 25–30%, e.g. two extra doses a week (RCOG 2025), and fertility assessment for both partners now, since 14 months of trying passes the 1-year point in NICE NG257 — without turning a results consultation into a fertility lecture
Hears the weight under "give me my life back" and asks rather than assumes; receives the conception disclosure as the real consultation, not a tangent
Meets the self-blame with warmth and fact, and gently suggests she not carry it alone — the husband, the shared load

Safety-nets and follows up: how levothyroxine is taken (empty stomach, apart from iron or calcium) and that benefit is gradual not overnight; an early TSH recheck booked (about 6 weeks here, then 3-monthly until stable per NICE NG145); symptoms of over-replacement (palpitations, tremor) to report; what to do the moment a pregnancy test is positive (contact us, dose up, urgent TFTs); review that holds both the thyroid and the trying-to-conceive

worked.txt: "Your thyroid — the little gland in your neck that sets your body’s tempo — has been running slow, and your immune system is the reason. It’s called Hashimoto’s, it’s common, and crucially it’s one of the most treatable things I see: we replace the hormone with a daily tablet and your tempo comes back up."

"One honest thing so you don’t lose heart: this won’t flip you back to normal overnight. Over a few weeks the fog lifts, the cold eases, the weight becomes easier to shift. We start the tablet, recheck the level in about six weeks, and fine-tune. You take it first thing, empty stomach, then breakfast half an hour later."

"Before I hand you a prescription — when you said you want your life back, I had a feeling there might be more riding on this than the tiredness. Is there anything else you’re hoping this explains? … (receiving it) Fourteen months. Thank you for telling me — because that changes what today is about."

"Here’s what I want you to hear clearly: an underactive thyroid can absolutely make conceiving harder and can affect a pregnancy — and that is the BEST news you could get today, because it means we’ve found something real and fixable. This isn’t your body being broken. It’s a treatable hormone level, and we’re treating it. For trying to conceive we aim the level in the lower part of the normal range, and the moment you’re pregnant we increase the dose straight away — by about a quarter — and check your bloods."

"You said ‘look at the state of me’ like it was your fault. It isn’t. This is your immune system, not your effort. And I’d gently say — you’ve been carrying the trying-and-not-yet alone, crying in the car. Your husband would want to carry half of that. You don’t have to be the only one holding it."

"So: start levothyroxine today, folic acid today, recheck in six weeks aiming the level lower because we’re planning for a baby. The second a test is positive you ring us that day — we increase the dose and check the bloods promptly, because that bit matters. And given fourteen months, I’ll start fertility checks for both you and your husband too. You came in for a tablet. You’re leaving with a plan that takes the real thing seriously."

f.learning: Overt primary hypothyroidism (high TSH, low T4, positive TPO = Hashimoto’s) in a young healthy adult is replaced with a full weight-based levothyroxine dose (NICE NG145: 1.6 micrograms/kg/day, rounded to the nearest 25 micrograms, in adults under 65 without cardiovascular disease), taken fasting, rechecked early and then 3-monthly until stable, and titrated to target. That is the easy half. The marks live in the hidden agenda: a tiredness appointment is really a 14-month conception story carrying self-blame and forum-fuelled fear. Surface it, then deliver the counter-intuitive reframe — finding treatable hypothyroidism is GOOD news for fertility, not a verdict of brokenness — and adjust the plan: pre-conception TSH aim ≤2.5 mU/L and a 25–30% dose increase (e.g. two extra doses a week) with prompt thyroid tests as soon as pregnancy is confirmed (RCOG Green-top Guideline, 2025), folic acid 400 micrograms (NICE NG247), and fertility assessment for both partners now (NICE NG257). Lift the blame with evidence and share the load.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG145 (thyroid disease) · RCOG Green-top Guideline: thyroid disorders in pregnancy (2025) · NICE NG247 (maternal and child nutrition) · NICE NG257 (fertility problems)
knowledge.summary: Overt autoimmune hypothyroidism in a fit 31-year-old: start full weight-based levothyroxine. The consultation is really about 14 months of trying to conceive, so plan for pregnancy from day one.

points.t: Raised TSH with low free T4 is overt primary hypothyroidism. Positive TPO antibodies point to autoimmune (Hashimoto’s) thyroiditis. It explains the tiredness, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation and heavier periods.

NICE NG145: for adults under 65 with no history of cardiovascular disease, consider starting levothyroxine at 1.6 micrograms/kg/day, rounded to the nearest 25 micrograms. Low-and-slow starting is for older people or those with heart disease.

BNF: take once daily on an empty stomach, usually 30 minutes before breakfast. Iron and calcium supplements reduce absorption, so keep them several hours apart; this includes pregnancy multivitamins containing iron.

NICE NG145: measure TSH every 3 months until stable (2 similar results in range 3 months apart), then yearly. TSH can take up to 6 months to settle after a very high level. Because she is trying to conceive, an earlier check to speed up titration is reasonable clinical judgement.

NICE NG145 does not cover pregnancy. RCOG 2025: for women with hypothyroidism on levothyroxine, aim for a TSH ≤2.5 mU/L pre-conception, then within the trimester-specific reference range; on a positive pregnancy test, increase the dose by about 25–30% (double the dose on two days each week, or increase by 25 micrograms/day if the pre-pregnancy dose is 100 micrograms/day or less, or 50 micrograms/day if more than 100) and check thyroid function promptly. Untreated hypothyroidism reduces fertility and harms pregnancy, so finding it is good news.

NICE NG247: 400 micrograms folic acid daily when planning pregnancy and until 12 weeks. NICE NG257: after 1 year of unprotected intercourse without conception, offer both partners clinical assessment and investigation. At 14 months she qualifies now.

dg.d: Asked what she already understood; invited other concerns early.
Work, relationship, 14 months trying to conceive, crying alone, what she has not told her husband.
Repeat TSH to titrate, earlier because she is trying to conceive; fertility assessment for both partners (NICE NG257).
Autoimmune primary hypothyroidism; other causes of fatigue already excluded (FBC, ferritin, B12, coeliac, glucose).
Asked about mood; recognised the pregnancy risk of untreated hypothyroidism.
Stated Hashimoto’s hypothyroidism in plain words, linked to her symptoms and fertility.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Full weight-based levothyroxine (NICE NG145); how to take it; folic acid; dose increase and bloods on a positive test (RCOG 2025).
Fertility assessment for both partners; iron-containing supplements kept apart from levothyroxine.
Blood test and review booked; over-replacement symptoms; ring the same day on a positive test.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “give me my life back”, the pause and “look at the state of me”, and explored them.
Idea (thyroid explains everything, maybe infertility), concern (it’s her fault, miscarriage), expectation (a tablet).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — 14 months of trying to conceive, self-blame ("my body doesn’t work"), and forum-fuelled fear that the thyroid means infertility or miscarriage even once treated — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Hana, I’m Dr Lee. Can you hear and see me all right? I know the receptionist mentioned your thyroid. Before I go through the results, what have you made of it so far?
model.why: Starts with her understanding before giving information

model.text: I googled it, so I’m half expecting you to say it explains why I feel like I’m wading through treacle. I just want to know whether there’s a tablet that gives me my life back.
That’s a good place to start. I’ll explain the results, talk about treatment, and make sure we cover anything else on your mind. Is there anything you want to be sure we get to?
model.why: Sets the agenda and invites other concerns early

model.text: No, just that really.
Tell me how things have been over the last few months.
Exhausted, all the time. I’ve put on five kilos without eating any differently. I wear a coat in the office. My skin’s dry, I’m constipated, and my brain’s just foggy.
How have your periods been, and your mood?
model.why: Completes the hypothyroid symptom review and opens a door

model.text: Heavier. And my mood’s been low. It’s… there’s just a lot going on.
You said you want your life back. I had a feeling there might be more riding on this than the tiredness. Is there something else you’re hoping it explains?
model.why: Picks up the cue behind “life back” and the pause

model.text: We’ve been trying for a baby for fourteen months. Nothing. I’ve decided it’s me. Look at the state of me.
Thank you for telling me. That changes what today is about. What have you read about the thyroid and pregnancy?
model.why: Receives the disclosure as the main agenda and explores her ideas

model.text: Forums. That it stops you getting pregnant, and even if you do, it causes miscarriages. I haven’t told my husband how much this is eating me. I cry in the car.
That’s a lot to carry on your own. What would you most like to come out of today?
model.why: Acknowledges the burden and elicits expectations

model.text: To know if this is why. And whether it’s my fault.

Your thyroid, the gland in your neck that sets your body’s pace, is running slow because your immune system has been attacking it. It’s called Hashimoto’s. It’s common, and it’s very treatable with a daily tablet that replaces the missing hormone.
model.why: Clear, jargon-free explanation of autoimmune hypothyroidism

model.text: So is it why I’m not pregnant?

It may well be part of it. An underactive thyroid can make conceiving harder and can affect a pregnancy. That’s why this is good news: we’ve found something real and fixable. It isn’t your fault, and it isn’t your body being broken. It’s a hormone level, and we can correct it.
model.why: Links hypothyroidism to fertility honestly and reframes the self-blame

model.text: I didn’t expect to feel relieved.
Can I check you’re not pregnant at the moment, as far as you know? When was your last period?
model.why: Checks current pregnancy status before planning the dose

model.text: Two weeks ago. I did a test last week anyway. Negative. I always do.

I’d like to start levothyroxine today at a full dose based on your weight. Take it first thing on an empty stomach, half an hour before breakfast, and keep it apart from any iron or calcium. The fog and the cold should ease over a few weeks, not overnight. I’ll check your level in about six weeks so we can adjust it quickly, because you’re planning a pregnancy.
model.why: Correct starting dose, administration, realistic timescale and early review

model.text: OK. And do I stop trying until it’s sorted?

Ideally we get the level into range first, and we can talk about that together. What matters most is this: the moment you have a positive test, ring us that day. We’ll increase the dose straight away and check your bloods, because a baby needs more thyroid hormone early on. Start folic acid today too.
model.why: Pregnancy dose-increase rule and folic acid

model.text: I can do that.

Fourteen months is also long enough for you and your husband to have fertility checks, alongside treating the thyroid. I can start those. And I wonder whether he’d want to share some of this with you.
model.why: Offers fertility assessment and gently addresses sharing the load

model.text: He would. I’ve just been putting a brave face on. I’ll tell him tonight.

If you get palpitations, shakiness or chest pain after starting, let me know, as the dose may be too high. I’ll book your blood test and a review, and send the fertility test forms. Can you tell me back the main points, so I know I’ve explained well?
model.why: Safety-net for over-replacement, dated follow-up and teach-back

model.text: Tablet every morning before breakfast, folic acid, bloods in six weeks. Positive test, I ring you the same day. And tests for both of us.
Perfect. You came in for a tablet, and you’re leaving with a plan for the thing that matters most to you.
model.why: Summarises and ties the plan to her agenda

model.text: Thank you. Honestly.

social.t: Fourteen months of trying, self-blame and crying alone. Relationship strain and low mood are common; ask about both and encourage shared support.
An accounts manager with brain fog. Recovery is gradual; she may want to adjust workload for a few weeks while treatment takes effect.

legal.t: In England, hypothyroidism needing thyroid hormone replacement qualifies for a medical exemption certificate. Pregnancy brings a separate maternity exemption.

professional.t: GMC Decision making and consent (2020): discuss the choice about trying to conceive while the dose is being optimised, and record her decision.
Give facts that answer her fear: autoimmune thyroid disease is not caused by anything she did, and treatment improves fertility and pregnancy outcomes.

community.t: British Thyroid Foundation for information on levothyroxine and pregnancy; Fertility Network UK for support; NHS Talking Therapies if low mood persists.

redFlags: Possible pregnancy now — needs same-day dose increase and thyroid function tests
Chest pain or known heart disease — would change the starting dose
Marked low mood or hopelessness — screen, given the infertility distress
psychosocial: Trying to conceive for 14 months; self-blame and forum fears
What she has shared with her husband
Impact of fog and fatigue on work
ice: Idea: her thyroid explains the exhaustion and maybe why she isn’t pregnant
Concern: it’s her fault; infertility or miscarriage even once treated
Expectation: a tablet to give her life back

playbook.diagnosis: Overt primary hypothyroidism due to autoimmune (Hashimoto’s) thyroiditis — TSH 22 mU/L, free T4 low, TPO antibodies positive — in a woman trying to conceive for 14 months.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your thyroid is like the thermostat for your body’s engine. Your immune system has turned it down. A daily tablet turns it back up. And getting it right helps your chances of pregnancy too.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been blaming yourself for not getting pregnant. This is your immune system, not anything you did, and it’s one of the most fixable things we find.”
management.psychosocial: Encourage her to share the worry with her husband; offer fertility assessment for both partners; check mood at review.
sharedPlan: Levothyroxine 1.6 micrograms/kg/day rounded to 25 micrograms (NICE NG145), taken fasting, apart from iron and calcium
Folic acid 400 micrograms daily (NICE NG247); positive test: increase dose 25–30% (e.g. two extra doses a week) and urgent TFTs (RCOG 2025)
Fertility assessment and investigation for both partners (NICE NG257)
safetyNet: Palpitations, tremor or chest pain after starting: contact the surgery
TSH check booked (earlier than the routine 3 months while trying to conceive); ring the same day on a positive test

pitfalls.intro: The thyroid part of this station is easy. It is failed by treating a tiredness appointment as just that, and by missing the pregnancy safety rule.

items.fail: Starting 25 micrograms “to be safe” in a fit 31-year-old.
items.why: NICE NG145 recommends a full weight-based starting dose in adults under 65 without heart disease.
items.fix: 1.6 micrograms/kg/day, rounded to the nearest 25 micrograms.

items.fail: No advice about what to do if she becomes pregnant.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” Thyroid hormone need rises early in pregnancy.
items.fix: “Positive test: ring us that day. We’ll increase the dose and check your bloods.”

items.fail: Ignoring 14 months of trying to conceive once it is disclosed.
items.why: NICE NG257: after 1 year, offer both partners assessment and investigation.
items.fix: Offer fertility tests for both partners now, alongside treating the thyroid.

items.fail: Handing over a prescription without asking what “give me my life back” means.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” The real agenda stays hidden.
items.fix: “It sounds like there’s more riding on this. Is there anything else you hope it explains?”

items.fail: Brushing past “look at the state of me”.
items.why: Self-blame drives her distress; leaving it unaddressed loses Relating marks.
items.fix: “This is your immune system, not your fault.”

items.fail: Jargon: “TPO-positive autoimmune thyroiditis with TSH 22; we’ll titrate to a target.”
items.why: “Language not easily understood by the patient.”
items.fix: “Your immune system has slowed your thyroid. A daily tablet replaces what it isn’t making.”

timeMap.d: Ask what she has made of the result. Invite anything else she wants to cover.
Tiredness, weight, cold, periods, mood. “Give me my life back” carries more weight; ask what else it might explain.
Fourteen months trying, forum fears, crying alone. Receive it as the real consultation.
Hashimoto’s, treatable; good news for fertility. Full-dose levothyroxine, how to take it, folic acid, positive-test rule, fertility checks for both.
Blood test booked, over-replacement symptoms, same-day call on a positive test, teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Prescribes 25 micrograms and closes; never asks why she is so desperate for her life back; misses the conception story; no pregnancy advice; or lectures on fertility statistics without addressing her self-blame.
wordPics.pass: Explains Hashimoto’s; starts levothyroxine correctly with a follow-up test; finds the conception agenda; advises folic acid and to contact the surgery if pregnant.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: reframes the diagnosis as fixable good news for fertility; lifts the blame; clear positive-test rule with dose increase; fertility assessment for both partners; encourages her to share the load with her husband; teach-back.

avoid.dont: “Your thyroid’s a bit underactive. I’ll start a small dose and we’ll see.”
avoid.instead: “This is Hashimoto’s. It’s common and very treatable. I’ll start a full dose based on your weight.”
avoid.why: Low-and-slow starting is for older or cardiac patients; it delays her recovery and her pregnancy plans.

avoid.dont: “Don’t worry about fertility, lots of people take a while.”
avoid.instead: “This may well be part of why. That’s good news, because it’s fixable, and it isn’t your fault.”
avoid.why: Generic reassurance ignores the self-blame she came in carrying.

avoid.instead: “The moment you have a positive test, ring us that day. We’ll increase the dose and check your bloods.”
avoid.why: Delay in increasing the dose in early pregnancy is the key safety failure.

SCA_STEM.name: Hana Yilmaz
SCA_STEM.recent: Seen three weeks ago for tiredness, weight gain and cold intolerance. Bloods: TSH 22 mU/L, free T4 7.1 pmol/L (low), TPO antibodies strongly positive. FBC, ferritin, B12, coeliac screen and glucose normal.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video appointment to discuss blood results.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG145 (thyroid disease) · RCOG Green-top Guideline: thyroid disorders in pregnancy (2025) · NICE NG247 (maternal and child nutrition) · NICE NG257 (fertility problems)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Overt autoimmune hypothyroidism in a fit 31-year-old: start full weight-based levothyroxine. The consultation is really about 14 months of trying to conceive, so plan for pregnancy from day one.

points.t: Raised TSH with low free T4 is overt primary hypothyroidism. Positive TPO antibodies point to autoimmune (Hashimoto’s) thyroiditis. It explains the tiredness, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation and heavier periods.

NICE NG145: for adults under 65 with no history of cardiovascular disease, consider starting levothyroxine at 1.6 micrograms/kg/day, rounded to the nearest 25 micrograms. Low-and-slow starting is for older people or those with heart disease.

BNF: take once daily on an empty stomach, usually 30 minutes before breakfast. Iron and calcium supplements reduce absorption, so keep them several hours apart; this includes pregnancy multivitamins containing iron.

NICE NG145: measure TSH every 3 months until stable (2 similar results in range 3 months apart), then yearly. TSH can take up to 6 months to settle after a very high level. Because she is trying to conceive, an earlier check to speed up titration is reasonable clinical judgement.

NICE NG145 does not cover pregnancy. RCOG 2025: for women with hypothyroidism on levothyroxine, aim for a TSH ≤2.5 mU/L pre-conception, then within the trimester-specific reference range; on a positive pregnancy test, increase the dose by about 25–30% (double the dose on two days each week, or increase by 25 micrograms/day if the pre-pregnancy dose is 100 micrograms/day or less, or 50 micrograms/day if more than 100) and check thyroid function promptly. Untreated hypothyroidism reduces fertility and harms pregnancy, so finding it is good news.

NICE NG247: 400 micrograms folic acid daily when planning pregnancy and until 12 weeks. NICE NG257: after 1 year of unprotected intercourse without conception, offer both partners clinical assessment and investigation. At 14 months she qualifies now.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Asked what she already understood; invited other concerns early.
Work, relationship, 14 months trying to conceive, crying alone, what she has not told her husband.
Picked up “give me my life back”, the pause and “look at the state of me”, and explored them.
Idea (thyroid explains everything, maybe infertility), concern (it’s her fault, miscarriage), expectation (a tablet).
Repeat TSH to titrate, earlier because she is trying to conceive; fertility assessment for both partners (NICE NG257).
Autoimmune primary hypothyroidism; other causes of fatigue already excluded (FBC, ferritin, B12, coeliac, glucose).
Asked about mood; recognised the pregnancy risk of untreated hypothyroidism.
Stated Hashimoto’s hypothyroidism in plain words, linked to her symptoms and fertility.
Full weight-based levothyroxine (NICE NG145); how to take it; folic acid; dose increase and bloods on a positive test (RCOG 2025).
Fertility assessment for both partners; iron-containing supplements kept apart from levothyroxine.
Blood test and review booked; over-replacement symptoms; ring the same day on a positive test.

social.t: Fourteen months of trying, self-blame and crying alone. Relationship strain and low mood are common; ask about both and encourage shared support.
An accounts manager with brain fog. Recovery is gradual; she may want to adjust workload for a few weeks while treatment takes effect.

legal.t: In England, hypothyroidism needing thyroid hormone replacement qualifies for a medical exemption certificate. Pregnancy brings a separate maternity exemption.

professional.t: GMC Decision making and consent (2020): discuss the choice about trying to conceive while the dose is being optimised, and record her decision.
Give facts that answer her fear: autoimmune thyroid disease is not caused by anything she did, and treatment improves fertility and pregnancy outcomes.

community.t: British Thyroid Foundation for information on levothyroxine and pregnancy; Fertility Network UK for support; NHS Talking Therapies if low mood persists.

redFlags: Possible pregnancy now — needs same-day dose increase and thyroid function tests
Chest pain or known heart disease — would change the starting dose
Marked low mood or hopelessness — screen, given the infertility distress

What she has shared with her husband
Impact of fog and fatigue on work
ice: Idea: her thyroid explains the exhaustion and maybe why she isn’t pregnant
Concern: it’s her fault; infertility or miscarriage even once treated
Expectation: a tablet to give her life back

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Overt primary hypothyroidism due to autoimmune (Hashimoto’s) thyroiditis — TSH 22 mU/L, free T4 low, TPO antibodies positive — in a woman trying to conceive for 14 months.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your thyroid is like the thermostat for your body’s engine. Your immune system has turned it down. A daily tablet turns it back up. And getting it right helps your chances of pregnancy too.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been blaming yourself for not getting pregnant. This is your immune system, not anything you did, and it’s one of the most fixable things we find.”
management.psychosocial: Encourage her to share the worry with her husband; offer fertility assessment for both partners; check mood at review.
sharedPlan: Levothyroxine 1.6 micrograms/kg/day rounded to 25 micrograms (NICE NG145), taken fasting, apart from iron and calcium
Folic acid 400 micrograms daily (NICE NG247); positive test: increase dose 25–30% (e.g. two extra doses a week) and urgent TFTs (RCOG 2025)
Fertility assessment and investigation for both partners (NICE NG257)
safetyNet: Palpitations, tremor or chest pain after starting: contact the surgery
TSH check booked (earlier than the routine 3 months while trying to conceive); ring the same day on a positive test

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The thyroid part of this station is easy. It is failed by treating a tiredness appointment as just that, and by missing the pregnancy safety rule.

items.fail: Starting 25 micrograms “to be safe” in a fit 31-year-old.
items.why: NICE NG145 recommends a full weight-based starting dose in adults under 65 without heart disease.
items.fix: 1.6 micrograms/kg/day, rounded to the nearest 25 micrograms.

items.fail: No advice about what to do if she becomes pregnant.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” Thyroid hormone need rises early in pregnancy.
items.fix: “Positive test: ring us that day. We’ll increase the dose and check your bloods.”

items.fail: Ignoring 14 months of trying to conceive once it is disclosed.
items.why: NICE NG257: after 1 year, offer both partners assessment and investigation.
items.fix: Offer fertility tests for both partners now, alongside treating the thyroid.

items.fail: Handing over a prescription without asking what “give me my life back” means.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.” The real agenda stays hidden.
items.fix: “It sounds like there’s more riding on this. Is there anything else you hope it explains?”

items.fail: Brushing past “look at the state of me”.
items.why: Self-blame drives her distress; leaving it unaddressed loses Relating marks.
items.fix: “This is your immune system, not your fault.”

items.fail: Jargon: “TPO-positive autoimmune thyroiditis with TSH 22; we’ll titrate to a target.”
items.why: “Language not easily understood by the patient.”
items.fix: “Your immune system has slowed your thyroid. A daily tablet replaces what it isn’t making.”
